analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal law requiring prevailing wages on federally funded construction projects.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors on federally funded construction of buildings and public works to pay workers the locally prevailing wage for their trade [S2]. This bill would wipe out that requirement, along with the related wage reporting rules, starting 30 days after enactment, though contracts already signed or bid out would keep the old terms [S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Steve King of Iowa with five Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee [S1][S4]. The committee sent it to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Government contractors on federally funded construction projects would gain, because they could bid using lower-wage labor instead of the locally prevailing wage. Supporters also argue taxpayers would save through lower bids, and that repealing the rules would cut paperwork for contractors and subcontractors [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act's requirement that federally financed construction pay the locally prevailing wage to laborers and mechanics [S2][S3].
Repeals the related wage-reporting requirement, reducing recordkeeping duties for government contractors [S3].
Takes effect 30 days after enactment but leaves existing contracts and bids already outstanding on the old terms [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federal projects would bear the cost: without the prevailing-wage rule, contractors would be free to pay less than the local rate for their trade. Union and nonunion building-trades workers who currently rely on federally financed work at prevailing rates would see that wage floor disappear [S2].

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the wage floor that guarantees workers on federally funded construction are paid the locally prevailing rate for their trade, exposing them to lower bids and pay cuts [S2].
The bill repeals not just the wage standards but the reporting requirement as well, removing the recordkeeping that lets the government verify what contractors actually pay [S3].

Supporters' case is that prevailing-wage rules raise the cost of federal construction and add paperwork for contractors and subcontractors; repeal would trade that cost saving directly against construction workers' pay, and the bill offers no transition help for affected workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to taxpayers and contractors would come almost entirely out of construction workers' paychecks on federal projects, and the bill would remove both the wage floor and the reporting rules used to check pay. Any taxpayer savings are a direct transfer from workers' wages.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act on December 18, 2005, with five Republican cosponsors: Reps. Blackburn, Musgrave, Feeney, Flake, and Hensarling [S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
On March 27, 2006, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, the last action the bill ever received [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded projects are better off, because the prevailing-wage requirement stayed on the books. Contractors who would have paid less never got the change they sought.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon wage requirements and its reporting rules.

for.name: Reps. Blackburn, Musgrave, Feeney, Flake, and Hensarling
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat is listed as a supporter [S4], but the bill never got a vote, so the full chamber's split was never tested.

industries.note: Repeal would let contractors on federally funded projects bid with lower-wage labor instead of the locally prevailing wage, cutting their labor costs at the direct expense of construction workers' pay. It would also end the wage-reporting paperwork they currently file.

industries.industry: Building trades unions and construction workers
industries.note: Davis-Bacon sets a wage floor for union and nonunion workers alike on federal construction; repeal would remove it, exposing workers to lower pay on government-funded jobs.
